catalog_quote: 2.5 Word-accent and sentence intonation. (i) Word-accent. Word-accent is predictable, the distinction being between accented and unaccented syllables. Accented syllables bear high pitch, unaccented syllables, low pitch. A phonological word is defined as one whose stem-initial syllable is prominent. Prominence is marked by raising the pitch level of the stem-initial syllable of a word, e.g. {tec} ['dɛc] nit, {wara} ['wä$ra] paperbark, {munnuk} ['mʊn$nʊk] toadfish, {warapel} ['wä$ra$βɛl] kangaroo sp., {panpapanpa} ['ban$ba$βan$ba] flat ... {parrkkatta+malaŋ} ['barrk$kat$ta$ma$laŋ] two ... [p. 41] Where the stem-initial syllable is not word-initial, as on verbs, pitch-raising spreads leftwards from the initial syllable of the stem, e.g. {yaŋ+pø+mene} ['yaŋ'$bø$mɛ$nɛ] 1sgA.3sgmO-hit-NF I hit him/it, {pilk+yaŋ+pø+mene} ['bɪlk$'yaŋ$'bø$mɛ$nɛ] slap-1sgA.3sgmO-hit-NF I slap/ped him/it. new_statements.rule_in_words: Word accent (realised as high pitch) is predictable and falls on the stem-initial syllable, which for nominals and other unprefixed words is the word-initial syllable; on prefixed verbs the high pitch extends leftward from the stem-initial syllable over the pronominal prefixes, so the left edge of the word is always high; all suffixes and enclitics are low/unaccented.
new_statements.secondary_stress: None described as such; on prefixed verbs Ford marks each syllable from the word start through the stem-initial syllable with the accent mark (leftward pitch spread), not a separate secondary accent.
new_statements.exceptions: Clitic + host and compounds form a single phonological unit (accent on the first element only); word-accent distinguishes a compound nominal ['bam$bac$ka$laŋ] 'woman with baby' from possessive juxtaposition ['bɪ$la$wuk # 'pam$bac] 'Bilawuk's baby'; initial CV of some clitic particles elides after host-final vowel. No lexical exceptions to stem-initial accent are given.
new_statements.domain_note: Domain is the phonological word (stem + suffixes + enclitics; compounds one unit); accent described in terms of pitch (high vs low), with Ford explicitly separating word-accent from sentence intonation (non-questions end low, questions end high). Examples are citation forms and short inflected verbs.
new_statements.identity_note: Ford describes 'Bachamal' (= Batjamalh/Batyamal), which she states is the name fluent speakers give to the language of the Wajiginy (Wadjiginy) tribe (Ford 1990:4-5); Tryon 1974:206-207 treats Batyamal as a sub-dialect of Wadyiginy sharing 90% cognates with near-identical grammar. Glottolog files both Ford 1990 and Ford 2016 under wadj1254, so no separate glottocode applies. Speakers at Belyuen (Delissaville), Cox Peninsula, NT.

sources.note: Sec. 2.5 pp.40-43: word-accent is predictable; the stem-initial syllable of a phonological word is prominent (high pitch); on prefixed verbs pitch-raising spreads leftward from the stem-initial syllable over the prefixes; inflectional/derivational suffixes and clitics are unaccented; compounds form one unit; accent distinguishes compound nominal from possessive juxtaposition.
